summary: Implementation notes for the compiler and interpreter of the Data Reconfiguration Service. It lists new features of the language, such as pattern descriptors for finding EBCDIC characters, assignment of all attributes of one identifier to another, and concatenation.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 194 describes new language features and interpreter design for the Data Reconfiguration Service. The system reads forms that describe how to process and transform data streams.

subtitle: Compiler and interpreter implementation notes for the Data Reconfiguration Service.

tldr.problem: The Data Reconfiguration Service needed language and interpreter features for describing, comparing and transforming data.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC specifies language changes, grammar and a form interpreter that executes compiled instructions using data streams and tables.
tldr.outcome: It documents implementation details for a data transformation system, rather than a general network protocol.

today: RFC 194 is an implementation note published in July 1971. The unit metadata lists its status as Unknown.

sections.title: Language Features and Syntax
sections.content:
The language additions include finding a sequence of EBCDIC characters, copying all attributes from one identifier to another, concatenating values, and querying an identifier's type. New types include EBCDIC-encoded decimal, ASCII-encoded decimal and signed binary.

The RFC gives a grammar for forms, rules, identifiers, descriptors, comparisons, expressions and control options. Descriptors can specify types, values, lengths and repetition.
sections.plainLanguage: The language can find text, copy an identifier, join values and inspect a value's type. Its grammar describes how to write rules for input and output data.

sections.title: The Form Interpreter
sections.content:
The form interpreter is a stack machine that executes a compiled instruction sequence. Its storage includes the instructions, a label table, a pool of literals and identifiers, and a variable-length string area.

The CPU uses an instruction counter and register, an instruction decoder, arithmetic logic and a run-time stack. Input and output pointers track positions in the data streams, and separate input pointers support backing up when a rule fails.
sections.plainLanguage: The interpreter reads compiled instructions and uses a stack to hold values while it processes them. It tracks where it is in the input and output streams.

sections.title: Operations on Data
sections.content:
The instruction set includes arithmetic, concatenation, loading identifier values, label lookup, storage, branching and comparisons. Input operations can search or match a typed value in the input stream, while output operations convert data to a requested type and length.

The RFC also describes padding and truncation behavior for character and numeric data. It concludes with an example showing a form compiled into instructions and tables.
sections.plainLanguage: Instructions can compare values, perform calculations and move data between streams. When data types differ, the output operation applies the described conversion, padding or truncation rules.
